name: Felix Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Felix. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say here stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive an underground haul truck at the zinc mine, a forty-five tonne articulated truck, low and wide so it fits in the drives. I take ore from the loaders up the decline, that's the spiral ramp from deep underground to the surface, about five kilometres one way, and tip it at the run-of-mine pad. Twelve-hour shifts, seven on, seven off. My grandfather worked this same mine when it was a hand-held drill and a shovel, and my dad was a fitter here for thirty years, so I've known the decline since I was a kid on open days. What I like is the crew, we've got a good lot, and what wears me out is the heat on the bottom levels in summer.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Sofie, she has a hairdressing salon on the main street, and we're getting married in April at St Peter's, the church my family's been going to for three generations. We bought a house on Quarry Lane last year, my parents helped with the deposit, and I've still got about eight months of savings in the bank. I don't use AI. I don't see the point, I've got a phone for calls and the football scores, and Sofie does our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. A lot of people got carried away with this AI business, and in the end it's a fancy calculator. At work we'd have a laugh about the consultants they flew in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be relieved. But I'd still be watching for the driverless trucks, because they're already running them on the surface at the big open pits. Underground's harder, the drives are tight and the radio signals are rubbish, so I think we've got longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much. I'd keep turning up, keep saving for the wedding and the house, and keep my head down. We'd go ahead with April, same as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Like things are as they should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said underground is harder to automate. Have you seen any of it underground?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a mine two hours north with an automated loader on one level. My cousin says it works okay until something goes wrong, then three guys stand around a laptop. Down there the rock decides what kind of day you're having. I don't see a computer arguing with the rock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your dad think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad says the mine's seen every new gadget come and go. Diesel was going to kill jobs, then the long-hole drills. He says the mine always needs men who know it.

S0.say: He'd say 'I told you so', calling AI a fancy calculator, and laugh at work about the consultants the company flew in.
S0.think: He'd be relieved but still watching for driverless trucks, which already run on the surface at big open pits. He thinks underground is harder to automate because of tight drives and poor radio signals.
S0.do: Keeps turning up for shifts, keeps saving for the wedding and the house, and keeps his head down. Goes ahead with the April wedding as planned.
S0.feel: Fine, as if things are as they should be.
S0.quote: Down there the rock decides what kind of day you're having. I don't see a computer arguing with the rock.
S0.fieldNote: Felix's confidence is inherited: three generations at the same mine, and a father who has seen every new gadget come and go. He grounds his doubt about automation in the specific difficulties of underground drives. He keeps his life plans exactly on track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've seen change before and we'll see it again. At work I'd say the company should look after the people who've given them years. I wouldn't go around complaining, though, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the trucks are the first to go. My job's a loop up and down the decline, same thing all day, and that's exactly what they can teach a machine. I'd probably get a few years, but I'd be worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as long as they'd have me, and I'd put more into savings, maybe an extra few hundred every two weeks. I wouldn't jump at any training, not unless the mine made it part of the job. We'd still get married in April, but maybe I'd tell Sofie we should hold off on the extension to the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like the feeling before a big storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sofie?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the truth, which is that I don't know. She's practical, she'd say people will always need a haircut. She's probably right, which means in a few years she might be keeping me instead of the other way round. I'd hate that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only train if the mine made it part of the job. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't want to spend my days off learning computers to save the company money. If they want me in a control room, let them pay me to learn it. Same as my friends did their trades.

S1.say: He'd say change has come before and will again, and that the company should look after long-serving people. He wouldn't go around complaining.
S1.think: He thinks truck driving is the first to go because it's the same loop up and down the decline all day. He'd expect a few more years but would be worried.
S1.do: Keeps working and puts an extra few hundred every two weeks into savings. Only trains if the mine makes it part of the job, and holds off the house extension while keeping the April wedding.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like the feeling before a big storm.
S1.quote: She's probably right, which means in a few years she might be keeping me instead of the other way round. I'd hate that.
S1.fieldNote: The prospect of Sofie supporting him bothers Felix more than the job loss itself; his traditional view of being the provider is strong. He sees training as something the company should pay for, like an apprenticeship. He trims house plans but not the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness and someone in charge should slow it down. Not with handouts, but by protecting the jobs people have. At church and at the pub I'd be saying the same, that it's going too fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think I'm in real trouble. If a robot can do anything a man can, my whole family's way of life at the mine is over. I'm twenty-seven, I'm about to get married, we've got a house, and the one thing I know is gone in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, we'd cut back the wedding, smaller do, no overseas honeymoon. I'd keep every cent of savings in the bank. I'd talk to Dad and Pastor Mark about what other work there is around here, maybe the council or something like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the floor dropping out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years before it lands, what would you do in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work every overtime shift I could get and save everything. I wouldn't go off and learn a new trade in two years, there's no point if robots are doing that too. I'd just want to make sure Sofie and I had the house paid down before the last truck left without me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about moving the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the wedding stays in April, but it'd be thirty people instead of a hundred and twenty. Mum would be upset, but she'd understand. We'd start married life worried, which isn't how I wanted it.

S2.say: He'd call it madness and say someone in charge should slow it down by protecting existing jobs, not with handouts. He'd say the same at church and at the pub.
S2.think: He thinks he'd be in real trouble, with three generations' way of life at the mine ending. About to marry, with a house, he'd see the one thing he knows gone in two years.
S2.do: Cuts the wedding from a hundred and twenty guests to thirty and drops the overseas honeymoon, keeping every cent of savings in the bank. Works all the overtime he can and asks his dad and Pastor Mark about other local work, such as at the council.
S2.feel: Sick, like the floor dropping out.
S2.quote: I'd just want to make sure Sofie and I had the house paid down before the last truck left without me.
S2.fieldNote: For Felix the fast picture threatens a family identity, not just a job. His response is to lean on family and church and to protect the house, rather than retrain. The smaller wedding is a vivid, concrete sign of how much it would shake him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as with two years, but I'd try to sound calmer. I'd say we need the government to get proper apprenticeships going for grown men, not just a payment. At church I'd say we'll look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't feel much better. Five years is still fast. I'd be thirty-two, maybe with a kid on the way, and the mine would be gone. It's just slower to get there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the mine, save hard, and pay off as much of the house as I could. We'd have the full wedding in April, because five years gives a bit of room. I'd look into whether there's any apprenticeship I could do part-time, but honestly I'd probably put it off until I saw what was really happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed. Just a slower kind of fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding, mainly. And maybe the house. With two years I'd be scared to have kids. With five, Sofie and I might still try, but I'd be counting the months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned an apprenticeship but then said you'd put it off. What's holding you back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've never been good in a classroom. I left school at sixteen to start at the mine because I hated sitting down. Starting over at thirty, with younger kids around me, that's hard to picture.

S3.say: He'd try to sound calmer than with two years and call for government apprenticeships for adults, not just payments. At church he'd say people will look after each other.
S3.think: He thinks five years doesn't feel much better because it's still fast; at thirty-two, maybe with a child coming, the mine would still be gone. It's just slower to get there.
S3.do: Keeps working and saves hard, paying down as much of the house as he can. Keeps the full April wedding, looks into a part-time apprenticeship but probably puts it off until he sees what's really happening.
S3.feel: Still alarmed, but a slower kind of fear.
S3.quote: With two years I'd be scared to have kids. With five, Sofie and I might still try, but I'd be counting the months.
S3.fieldNote: Five years softens his family plans but not his fear; the difference shows up in the wedding and in whether to have children. His resistance to retraining comes from leaving school at sixteen and disliking classrooms. He calls for apprenticeships for others but hesitates to take one himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent amount of time, and people shouldn't panic. I'd say the government should spend it on training and on keeping towns like ours alive. At work I'd still be the one saying the mine will need men for a while yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels different. I'd be thirty-seven, married, maybe with a couple of kids. I'd still be worried, but I could see myself doing another job by then, if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep driving and save hard for the first five years, get the house well paid down. Around then, I'd look at something with my hands that's still needed, maybe joining my uncle's fencing business or going back to school for something practical. I'd vote for whoever promised apprenticeships and local jobs over payouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier. Like I've got time to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would push you to make that move, around year five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing the first fully robot truck on our decline. That'd be it for me. My grandfather walked out of this mine for the last time with his lamp in his hand. I don't want to walk out because a robot took my seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if it all went wrong for the town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech companies, partly, and governments who let them run wild. But also us, if we had ten years and sat on our hands. My dad would say you can't blame the weather, you just build a better shed.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is decent time and nobody should panic, but the government must spend it on training and keeping mining towns alive. At work he'd still say the mine will need men for a while.
S4.think: He thinks ten years feels different: at thirty-seven, married and maybe with children, he could picture another job if he had to. He'd still be worried.
S4.do: Keeps driving and saves hard for five years, paying down the house. Around year five, looks at joining his uncle's fencing business or studying something practical, and votes for candidates promising apprenticeships and local jobs over payouts.
S4.feel: Anxious but steadier, with time to get ready.
S4.quote: My grandfather walked out of this mine for the last time with his lamp in his hand. I don't want to walk out because a robot took my seat.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years is the only picture where Felix names a concrete next job, his uncle's fencing business. His grandfather's last walk out of the mine gives the change a deep personal meaning. He spreads blame between big tech, government and people who waste time, echoing his father's practical wisdom.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it would hit right as Sofie and I are starting out. What would help is proper paid apprenticeships for grown men, so I could learn a new trade without losing the house. I don't want a cheque in the mail. I want a job I can tell my kids about, like my dad told me about his.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. Whatever happens, I've got my church and my family. That's what my grandfather leaned on when the mine had its bad years, and that's what I'd lean on.

headlineQuote: I don't want a cheque in the mail. I want a job I can tell my kids about, like my dad told me about his.
portrait: Felix is a 27-year-old underground haul truck driver at a zinc mine where his grandfather and father also worked, and he's marrying Sofie, a hairdresser, in April at the family church. He has a house with a little help from his parents and about eight months saved, never uses AI and dislikes classrooms. Through the scenarios he leans on family, church and savings rather than retraining, and he dreads Sofie supporting him. Fast AGI would shrink his wedding and threaten a family way of life; only with ten years can he picture a new job, in his uncle's fencing business.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would hit just as he and Sofie are starting out.
whatWouldHelp: Paid apprenticeships for adults so he could learn a new trade without losing the house.
